analysis.one_liner: Limits the number of patents brand-name biologic makers can use to sue copycat competitors and delay cheaper versions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in July 2024 and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name biologic drug's patents near expiration, makers often pile up new patents on small changes and sue biosimilar competitors, delaying cheaper versions for years — a practice called 'product hopping.' This bill would cap, at 20 patents, how many a brand maker can assert in one lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant. It never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who take expensive biologic drugs (used for conditions like arthritis, cancer, and diabetes), because faster biosimilar competition typically brings lower prices. Biosimilar makers also gain by facing a bounded patent fight instead of a lawsuit listing dozens or hundreds of patents.

how_it_helps.text: Caps at 20 the number of patents a brand-name biologic maker can assert in an infringement lawsuit against a biosimilar applicant, with no more than 10 patents issued after a statutory deadline, curbing 'patent thickets' used to run out the clock on litigation.
Extends the infringement framework so the same cap and rules apply to biological products, closing a route brand makers could use to argue the cap did not reach biosimilar litigation.
Lets courts raise the cap beyond 20 patents only on request and for good cause, such as a biosimilar applicant withholding required information — but the default limit stands.
Appropriates $1.8 billion into the Medicare Improvement Fund, which funds Medicare improvements (the fund currently has a $0 balance in statute).

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name biologic drug makers, whose patent leverage against biosimilar competitors would shrink, potentially shortening the period they can charge monopoly prices. Taxpayers bear a modest $1.8 billion Medicare Improvement Fund appropriation.

drawbacks.text: The cap does not apply to patents claiming a method of using the drug in therapy or treatment, so brand makers could still assert those patents without limit.
The cap can be raised by a court for 'good cause,' and 20 patents is still a very large lawsuit — the litigation burden on biosimilar makers remains substantial even if the bill passed.
The changes apply only to biosimilar applications filed after enactment, so pending cases and existing patent strategies are unaffected.
It appropriates $1.8 billion to the Medicare Improvement Fund with no stated connection to the patent provisions, an unrelated spending addition in the same bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the benefits would likely be real but partial: a 20-patent cap plus a carve-out for method-of-use patents limits, but does not end, the patent-stacking tactics that delay cheaper biosimilars. The cost falls on brand-name drug companies' patent leverage, and the unrelated Medicare Improvement Fund spending is a minor add-on. On balance a good-faith, if modest, attempt to speed drug price competition.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees at introduction in July 2024, its health-related provisions went to a Judiciary subcommittee in December 2024, and it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Darrell Issa (R-CA) introduced H.R. 9070 on July 18, 2024, joining it with Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia.
The bill was referred the same day to the Judiciary, Ways and Means, and Energy and Commerce Committees.
On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was taken.
It drew 2 cosponsors, both Democrats, and never received a committee markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic drug makers are better off because the bill died: they keep full freedom to assert large numbers of patents against biosimilar competitors and delay cheaper versions, leaving patients paying monopoly prices longer.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican sponsor was joined by two Democratic cosponsors, but with only three members behind it, the bill never reached the stage where a party-line fight could occur.

industries.note: The bill would cap the patents they can assert against biosimilar applicants at 20 per lawsuit, weakening the patent thicket that delays cheaper competitors. Their gain from the bill's death is continued monopoly pricing that patients pay for.
A bounded patent dispute lowers litigation cost and risk, making it easier to launch biosimilars whose entry typically lowers drug prices for patients. The bill died before they could benefit.
